title: Bali Pratipada: the demon king welcomed home
hookLine: the morning after the Lakshmi night, lamps welcome back Bali, a demon king honored for keeping his word
carry: a demon king honored for keeping his word

lines: THE MORNING AFTER THE LAKSHMI NIGHT.
cards: Diwali has a morning after. The Lakshmi night is done, and in Maharashtra and Karnataka families light lamps again, this time for a king coming home. Not Rama.
Bali, a demon king, an asura, the one the gods defeated. In Maharashtra some say a line that goes, roughly: let troubles go, and let Bali's kingdom come. So why would anyone light lamps for a demon?

teach.h: VAMANA: A BOY ASKS FOR THREE STEPS.
teach.b: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. Bali, grandson of Prahlad, the boy from the Holi fire, has grown so powerful and so generous that he rules all three worlds, and the gods have lost their places.
Vishnu comes to restore the balance as Vamana, a small boy, a young brahmin student with an umbrella and a water pot, at a great sacrifice Bali is holding. Bali is known for never refusing a guest.
Ask for anything, he says. The boy asks for three steps of land, measured by his own feet. Bali laughs: ask for more.
But Bali's teacher, Shukra, sees through it and warns him: this is Vishnu, and he'll take everything.
Bali gives anyway. I promised, he says, and I won't take back my word. Then the boy grows.

teach.h: THE THIRD STEP ON BALI'S HEAD.
teach.b: One step covers the earth, the second the heavens, and there's nowhere left for the third. So Bali bows and offers his own head.
Vishnu sends him down to a lower realm, Sutala, but praises his truthfulness and promises to stand guard at his door himself. That's the teaching under the lamps.
In Hindu stories, the side you're born on doesn't settle who is good. Bali is an asura, and so was Prahlad, and the Bhagavata names both among the Lord's great devotees.

teach.h: SATYA AND DANA: TRUTH AND GIVING.
teach.b: What it honors is satya, truthfulness, and dana, giving, kept even when they cost a kingdom.
So on Bali Pratipada, a family lighting a lamp at the door is honoring a king for what he did, not for where he came from.

how: In Maharashtra, Karnataka and nearby regions, the day after the main Diwali night is kept as Bali Pratipada, honoring King Bali's yearly return; in many places it is also a new-year day and a day of gifts between husbands and wives.

s: Bali refuses Vamana after Shukra's warning
he gives anyway: he won't take back his word.
Bali is an asura, yet the Bhagavata counts him among the great devotees
like his grandfather Prahlad: what counts is what he did, not his side.
the Bhagavata ends Bali's story as a simple punishment
Vishnu praises his truthfulness and promises to guard his door himself.

games.q: you're King Bali. you've promised a boy three steps of land. your teacher warns you the boy is Vishnu and will take everything. what do you do?
games.why: Bali keeps his word. two steps cover earth and heaven, and he offers his own head for the third.

practice: Light a lamp at your door, or picture one, the way families do for Bali's visit. If you pray, offer it to Vishnu, who keeps Bali's door. Then bring to mind someone you've quietly filed as the other side.
Look for one true good thing they do, the way the lamp looks past Bali's side to his word. Hold it for a few breaths.
